author: Nick Robins-Early
description:
Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation

Mark Zuckerberg published a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views on artificial intelligence and announced several plans for how Meta would develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-source AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer.

Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled “The Future is for Everyone,” Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian visi
title: Zuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta drops open-source model

author: Brian Logan
description:
Gilded Balloon Teviot
Performer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy show

‘Welcome to the most controversial show on the fringe!” Some audiences will diagnose self-regard in that intro by rookie standup Amanda Knox. For others, as for Knox herself, it merely acknowledges the continuing efforts to silence her. But then, Knox is “the human version of the blue/gold dress”, a canvas on to which we all project guilty, innocent – or weird. Her innocence now proved, it’s the last of these charges she takes on in this fringe outing, retelling her oft-told tale through the lens of new motherhood.

Is it a disgrace that she’s telling it at all – and prof
title: Amanda Knox in Cartwheel review – rookie standup acquitted of murder tells her story

author: PA Media
description:
• Spurs will play Charlton, Preston v Everton

  • Brentford away at Birmingham; Ipswich v Leicester

Five-time winners Chelsea have been handed a home draw against League One Luton in the second round of the Carabao Cup. Chelsea’s new manager, Xabi Alonso, will begin the club’s attempt to win the competition for the first time since 2015 later this month.

Fellow Premier League side Tottenham have also benefited from a home draw, against Championship opponents Charlton. The 11 top-tier sides not involved in European competition enter the draw in the second round, with the remaining nine following in round three.

Continue reading...
title: Carabao Cup second-round draw: Chelsea host Luton, Forest at home to Leeds

author: Sean Ingle at Alexander Stadium
description:
• 24-year-old secures title in 11.00sec in Birmingham

  • Norway win 4x400m mixed relay, Britain second

Britain’s Amy Hunt sprinted to women’s 100m glory to take a brilliant gold at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham. The 24-year-old came into the event as favourite, having won world silver over 200m in Tokyo and 100m at the Commonwealth Games a fortnight ago – and she delivered in emphatic style.

Hunt is never the quickest starter. In truth, she started like a woman whose spikes had been superglued to her blocks. But she came through at the finish to win in 11.00sec. Ewa Swoboda of Poland took silver in 11.02 and Delphine Nkansa claimed bronze for Belgium in 11.06.

Continue reading...
title: Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd

author: Anya Ryan
description:
Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh
With the air of a hungover postmortem, Richardson gives a head-spinning account of an encounter with an older comedian

If you’re partial to a bit of gossip and scandal, Harriet Richardson is your girl. In this gloriously juicy debut hour, she dishes the dirt on the DMs she received from an older comedian and the intense, utterly absorbing events that followed. Yes, she found his eBay account. And yes, she spent six months tracking him down on a dating app only to play his profile song hundreds of times. But what else is a girl driven by obsession supposed to do?

We meet Richardson, who until now has worked primarily as a performance artist, all smiles and ready to share. She takes us back to the creation of her 2024 viral piece 100 Dates, in which she spent Valentine’s Day online speed-dating in an attempt to analyse her relationship with infa
title: Harriet Richardson: Creep review – a scandalous delve into shame and desire

author: Guardian staff
description:
Loyalist sworn in after Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation Saturday morning

Todd Blanche has been sworn as US attorney general, cementing Donald Trump’s installation of his former personal attorney in charge of the Department of Justice.

Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was confirmed in his new position during a ceremony at the White House on Monday.

Continue reading...
title: Todd Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, sworn in as US attorney general

author: Nils Pratley
description:
Door was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliament

  • Thames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government department

Anybody who followed the supposed “clampdown” on bankers’ bonuses after the great financial crash in 2008 knew what to expect when water company bosses became a similar target for a bash in the bonus department. We would see the waterbed principle in action: when you push down in one area of remuneration, such as the performance-related stuff, another tends to go up.

Back in the day, banks invented “role-based allowances” – salary top-ups – to “compensate”, as they put it, their top earners for being subject to EU caps on bonuses. No executive was seriously inconvenienced by forgoing the chance of an astronomical (but not gu
title: Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect? | Nils Pratley

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dr Kate Martin is encouraged by the new network of community clinics, while Prof Dr John R Ashton says the forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp the nettle, while Marjorie Wallace expresses concerns about plans to cut mental health jobs in the NHS

It’s very encouraging to hear the announcement about the new network of community mental health clinics in England (Editorial, 6 August). The focus on early intervention is crucial, as it means that people can access treatment as early as possible, rather than waiting for their mental health to reach a crisis point. The centres should improve access, reaching people where they are. The government should make sure that they meaningfully involve people with lived experience of mental h
title: Mental health: one step forward and two steps back? | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Reading the memoir Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty – an issue that still blights the lives of countless young people today, says Sarah Schofield

Adrian Chiles’s emotional response to Poor by Katriona O’Sullivan really resonated with me (I’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbing, 30 July). I read it and my heart both sobbed and cheered for Katriona’s younger self and the woman she has become.

With its linear narrative, rich cultural references and “rags-to-riches” form, it might be taken for a tale of “that was then but this is now”. However, the defining part of the book is the epilogue, making clear that Katriona’s account of growing up in grinding, abject poverty is a story of then and now. Every day, countless Katrionas enter schools with “pissy pants”
title: Katriona O’Sullivan’s story of growing up in poverty is one that we can all learn from | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
There are serious political and societal messages to be found in some of the best-known fictional accounts of village cricket, argues Rod Edmond

Your leader (The Guardian view on sporting fair play: it was never quite cricket, 30 July) recycles the persistent caricature of Siegfried Sassoon’s, Hugh de Sélincourt’s and AG Macdonell’s cricket fiction as existing in a “bucolic dreamworld”.

Sassoon’s The Flower Show Match is set against the background of the Boer war, with recurring references to the relief of Ladysmith. The home umpire is also suspected of using his wooden leg to make dents in the pitch.

Continue reading...
title: The cricket fiction of Sassoon and De Sélincourt isn’t in a ‘bucolic dreamworld’ | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Health concerns | Rubbish decisions | In sympathy | Funeral songs | Short illnesses

Calls for changes to breast cancer guidelines for GPs are welcome (Report, 4 August). The existing guidelines are irrational. If your grandmother and mother have both had breast cancer, you are still not added to the intensified screening list unless an aunt or great-aunt or sister has also had breast cancer. Hence the system discriminates against families – like mine – with only one woman in a generation.
Helen Hills
York

• It seems that Anna Tims’s correspondent committed the wrong environmental crime (I was fined £500 after putting a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a full bin, 3 August). Instead of unwitti
title: Breast cancer screening guidelines discriminate against families like mine | Brief letters

author: Clive Paget
description:
Festival theatre, Edinburgh
Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s new music theatre work boasts a richly textured score with a direct but sophisticated musical language. Daniela Mack is ideal as the conflicted doctor as its heart

Despite singing dogs and a chorus of hallucinogenic sheep, Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek’s The Galloping Cure is not for the faint-hearted. Based on an original story by Karen Russell, itself inspired by Kafka’s A Country Doctor, the opera tells how a charismatic sideshow huckster rids a rural town of pain only to replace it with something far more sinister in a thinly veiled allegory of America’s opioid crisis. It’s a typically confronting slice of music theatre from the creators of
title: The Galloping Cure review – powerful new opera tackles the opioid crisis with bite and black comedy

author: Tom Garry
description:
• Former England midfielder keen for north-east to thrive

  • Newcastle have made ambitious signings this summer

Jordan Nobbs says winning promotion to the Women’s Super League with Newcastle would be “job done” for her footballing wishlist and would fulfil a personal ambition to see a club from the north-east play in the top tier.

Nobbs, who has 71 England caps, was born in Stockton-on-Tees and believes women’s football in the region would benefit immensely from top-flight representation. Newcastle finished sixth in WSL2 last term, 11 points behind the title winners, Birmingham, and nine points off the playoffs, but this summer they have made their promotion hopes clear with a flurry of high-calibre signings from the top division, including the striker Martha Thomas from Tottenham and the Liverpool du
title: Jordan Nobbs ready to wrap wishlist with Newcastle WSL dream: ‘It would be job done’

author: Alexandra Coghlan
description:
Tenebrae, Nigel Short / Anu Komsi and Sakari Oramo
St George’s Bristol / Bristol Beacon
Sunday afternoon’s two concerts, closing the Proms’ Bristol weekend, brought the superlative Tenebrae, and Sakari Oramo swapping baton for bow to duet with his wife

Ritual can be a choir in procession in a great cathedral or the simple act of putting down a violin bow. At the BBC Proms’ Bristol performances this weekend, it was both – and to strikingly different effect.

First, grandeur and spectacle, as Nigel Short and his chamber choir Tenebrae celebrated their 25th anniversary with a return to their 2005 commission: Joby Talbot’s Path of Miracles. Inspired by the Catholic pilgrimage to Santiago, it’s a piece with a cult following, a phenomenon as much as a score, and one that only comes to life fully in live performance.
title: Joby Talbot’s Path of Miracles / György  Kurtág’s Kafka Fragments review – Bristol Proms reach for the heavenly

description: In a mailbag edition of his newsletter, Jonathan Wilson answers questions about Michael Carrick, VAR and the Premier League’s new teams
title: Are Manchester United returning to relevance under Michael Carrick? | Jonathan Wilson

author: Maggie Zhou
description:
I loved the business of selling toys – it felt like I was selling joy. But my least favourite part was the gendered language

I was 15 when I landed my job at Toys R Us. Before that, my first job was a one-month stint at the local fish and chip shop, where I was paid in $20 bills slotted into Chiko roll packets. After a burn on my forearm (I still have it), I left the gig. That was the end of my hospitality career.

This was 2014. I knew my strengths and weaknesses; I was no good with deep-fry baskets or carrying more than one thing in each hand. I wanted to work in the hallowed halls of retail.

Continue reading...
title: A job that changed me: Working at a toy store was my teen feminist awakening

author: Kate Wyver
description:
Summerhall, Edinburgh
Jessica Aszkenasy rages and wrestles with daddy issues in a show that combines feminist analysis with outrageous humour and tenderness

After the 2025 debut of her breast-forward stage persona Titclown, Jessica Aszkenasy’s second grubbily smutty clowning show rolls around sardonically in daddy issues and the messy disappointment of men these days.

The straight dating pool is running dry. All this clown wants is a boyfriend, but none of them are enough like her father. As voice notes to friends unpack the feminist implications of wanting a man while generally disliking them, the Philippe Gaulier-trained clown wriggles around on the floor in an oversized suit with something bulging down below. Directed by Cecily Nash, Daddy’s Little Girl is divided neatly between these two forms: half wry analysis told w
title: Titclown: Daddy’s Little Girl review – a smart swipe at the mess made by men

author: Ranjana Srivastava
description:
My patients’ needs are varied and complex. Each interaction leaves a residue until the individual concerns blur into a dense mass, most requiring medical oversight

The other day, I made a mistake at work.

It was the end of a long day. I had already run an outpatient cancer clinic with dozens of unwell patients and then moved on to inpatient rounds on a busy medical unit.

Continue reading...
title: At the end of a long day I made a mistake at work. No patient was harmed and yet it weighs on me | Ranjana Srivastava

author: Ben Fisher
description:
• Referee was controversially refused entry to US in June

  • He will take charge of PSG v Aston Villa on Wednesday

The Somali referee Omar Artan, who was refused entry to the US to officiate at the World Cup, has spoken publicly for the first time about the decision and detailed his pride as he prepares to take charge of Wednesday’s Super Cup between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa. Uefa awarded Artan the game days after the 34-year-old was prevented from working at this summer’s tournament.

Artan will make history in Salzburg by becoming the first non-European official to take charge of Uefa’s annual competition between the Champions League winners and the Europa League champions. “When we got this call it was, for me and my family, really a very, very happy moment,” said Artan, who is considered one of Africa
title: Somali referee Omar Artan grateful for Super Cup chance after ‘tough’ World Cup exclusion

author: Lucy Pavia
description:
Whether it’s expensive regrets or brilliant bargains, we celebrate the stars’ shopping secrets – and the products that tempted you

• Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Like snooping in someone else’s supermarket trolley, discovering other people’s shopping habits satisfies a certain nosiness. And never more so than when it comes to celebrities – there’s nothing more human than knowing Kim Cattrall loves fish and chips, or that Henry Holland is a Skims guy.

And as celebrities often have the inside track – or perhaps we just think they do – on everything from coffee machines to skincare, their recommendat
title: From M&S pants to fancy skincare: the celebrity shopping recommendations you loved the most

author: Julia Kollewe
description:
Amid world pressure from heatwaves and fertiliser shortages, billionaire’s business has invested in circular farming and biomethane

There is a distinctive smell of cow manure in the air at the Duke of Westminster’s dairy farm near Chester. It is a world away from the collection of grand West End properties controlled by the duke that form the backbone of his near £10bn fortune, a decade on from becoming Britain’s youngest billionaire.

As part of his 349-year-old Grosvenor empire, Lea Manor Farm on the duke’s Eaton Estate in north-west England has fared better than most dairy farms in recent years.
title: ‘It’s very challenging’: how the Duke of Westminster’s farm is taking on the climate crisis

author: Hilary Osborne Money and consumer editor
description:
From ticket booking fees to parking, here are six other things he could fix

Andy Burnham has announced he will ban fake discounts and make it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions in an effort to improve life for UK consumers.

In the long run, these changes may not make as much difference to your wealth as increasing mandatory contributions on pensions or capping rents, but they will get rid of some day-to-day frustrations. Here are six other things he could fix while he is in the mood:

Continue reading...
title: After Burnham’s ‘rip-offs’ crackdown, what more could PM do to help us save money?

The Guardian’s picture editors select photographs from around the world

author: Mark Fisher
description:
Traverse theatre, Edinburgh
Writer-director Eilidh Loan takes inspiration from her grandmother for this portrait of grief and religion

Eilidh Loan marked her arrival as a playwright with Moorcroft, a tremendous male-centred comedy inspired by her father’s amateur football team. Now she has moved up a generation to write a female-centred family comedy inspired by her grandmother.

It was the older woman who stipulated that her character – the Cathy of the title – should be played by Elaine C Smith, a decision so spot on it suggests that she missed her calling as a casting director. It’s hard to imagine an actor who could better embody Loan’s vision of a newly widowed working-class woman whose grief is veering towards depression. She lands Loan’s jokes – acerbic and sharp – with battle-hardened precision.

At
title: Cathy review – snappy comedy with a perfect role for Elaine C Smith

author: Hugh Morris
description:
The New Orleans native is a three-time Grammy winner at the top of his game – and is now using his instinctive style to celebrate the resilience and clarity of Katrina survivors

‘Black music is forward and upward in movement, you know? Never forward or upward,” pianist Sullivan Fortner declares. “It’s a tornado that’s always getting bigger and moving faster,” he adds, whizzing his fingers around with delight.

On a video call between sets at Rotterdam’s North Sea jazz festival, the 39-year-old speaks like he plays, with quirkiness, subtlety and mischief. A three-time Grammy winner – including for 2025’s Southern Nights – Fortner also recently received the Larry J Bell award, a prize of $300,000 (£225,000) given every four years to a standout jazz pianist, which gave him the confidence to present an all-encompassi
title: ‘For this record, I took an edible and said, screw it’: jazz pianist Sullivan Fortner on confronting the trauma of Hurricane Katrina

author: Georgina Hayden
description:
A quick, takeaway-style chicken dish full of spice and flavour, with a homemade plum sauce, to serve with pancakes or rice

I have a real aversion to the term “fakeaway”. I don’t know why. But as much as I resist the terminology, I guess it’s exactly what this dish is – it’s 100% based on and inspired by a Chinese takeaway classic: crispy duck pancakes. A real people pleaser, and something my girls adore. Making this with pan-fried chicken takes next to no time and is the perfect after-school/work quick dinner. And for a different ending, I sometimes serve the chicken and plum sauce over jasmine rice instead. With the same accompaniments, of course.

Continue reading...
title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for spiced sticky chicken with plums and pancakes

author: Simon Hattenstone
description:
Political leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own lives

In January 2015, Tommy Nicol told his family that he was suffering “psychological torture of a person who is doing 99 years”. Nicol had been given an imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentence six years earlier for stealing a car from a garage and injuring the owner. He was already two years beyond his four-year tariff – the minimum time you can serve in prison before being considered for release. Nicol was given another two-year knock-back from the Parole Board and was in despair. If and when he got released, he would be on a lifelong licence. Eight months later, aged 37, Nicol hanged himself at The Mount prison in Hertfordshire, England.

By the time he took his own life, the inhumane I
title: Prison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him that | Simon Hattenstone

author: Matthew Weaver
description:
Ninety vehicles confiscated in weekend operation including rare Ferrari Monza SP2, driven by someone without insurance or full licence

A police officer got the opportunity to drive an open-top limited edition Ferrari in Mayfair, London, after the car was seized as part of a record-breaking crackdown on uninsured vehicles and dangerous driving.

The Dubai-registered supercar, worth £3.7m, had been in the UK for just a day when it was confiscated by the police because it was being driven by someone with a provisional licence and no insurance.

Continue reading...
title: Police officer gets chance to drive £3.7m Ferrari seized in Met crackdown

author: Gabrielle Canon
description:
Extreme conditions in Washington and Oregon have fueled fast-moving fires, leaving the region draped in toxic plumes – and the danger isn’t over

Piles of twisted metal and ashen debris line the cul-de-sacs where the tranquil suburbs of Spokane, Washington, once stood.

The scale of devastation from a historic fire season of wildfire in the Pacific north-west has come into sharper focus as firefighters wrangle a trio of blazes that consumed at least 846 structures on the eastern side of the state.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Unprecedented, dangerous territory’: US north-west reckons with a summer of historic wildfires

author: Arifa Akbar
description:
Summerhall, Edinburgh
Hannah Reilly is a bold and deft performer in a knotty solo show that questions whether sexual empowerment can survive its commodification

It is hard to ignore the buzz around Roleplay, which is star-producer Francesca Moody’s latest fringe find (previous wins: Baby Reindeer and Fleabag) and has queues around the corner. An erotic dance intro fulfils the promise of its racy poster but does the production actually live up to its hype?

In the end, yes, even if at first it seems to be marketed on exactly the thing it seeks to critique. Australian writer-performer Hannah Reilly’s one-woman show features Danielle, or Danni, whose podcast (tagline: “hey slut”) is near-ambushed by a producer who
title: Roleplay review – Fleabag producer scores again with one woman’s life as a ‘slutfluencer’

author: Guardian stage
description:
‘Spectacular’ or ‘stolid’? The reviews are in for the Royal Shakespeare Company’s prequel to George RR Martin’s fantasy blockbuster

You don’t need to read the entrails of a raven to guess the target of the subtitle The Mad King: the various Brutuses plotting his fall conclude that the “paranoid and delusional” monarch will destroy their civilisation. The focus, though, is not just Trumpian. Macmillan references two wider international crises – the instability of heads of state and the weather – and a UK national concern: the endurance of a royal bloodline. The RSC’s patron, King Charles III, might skip this one.

Mark Lawson, the Guardian

The main auditorium has been reconfigured so that the audience presses in on all sides with the action predominantly confined to a cruciform stage with mighty gates at the far end and a coro
title: ‘Makes Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey seem understated’ – critics weigh up Game of Thrones: The Mad King

author: Aamna Mohdin
description:
Performer on his Edinburgh show and how a growing wave of Palestinians are using comedy to tell their stories

The war in Gaza is a topic many avoid discussing, let alone joke about. But for Palestinian comedians, humour has become an essential tool for keeping life going while loved ones live under occupation and bombardment.

“A lot of Palestinian solidarity events are, rightfully, about grieving,” said the British Palestinian comedian Sami Abu Wardeh. “They’ll read out the names of children and all these atrocities, and then you leave depressed. We have to avoid that at all costs.”

Continue reading...
title: UK Palestinian comic Sami Abu Wardeh: ‘I committed the cardinal sin of comedy’

author: Emma Beddington
description:
Truman Capote had a ‘crow bro’; Dickens had a raven. And I get standoffish Susan, who has never brought me a present or perched on my shoulder

One of the greatest failures of my life to date (along with my sons’ shameful inability to eat apples correctly, down to the core) is my inability to attract a “crow bro”. That’s a corvid companion, and more and more people apparently have them, including Washington Post journalist Caitlin Gibson, who recently wrote about hers, Cormac, a charismatic fish crow with a taste for cashews.

It’s not a new phenomenon – Charles Dickens had a pet raven, Grip; Truman Capote had a crow called Lola – but thanks to
title: I should be happy to have a pigeon for a friend. But she wouldn’t be my first choice | Emma Beddington

author: Lucy O’Brien
description:
Andy Burnham and his social media team know how to connect with us. We’re no fools, though – this has to be backed by serious policies

Strapped up in his navy suit, blue tie and charmingly nerdy glasses, Andy Burnham entered No 10 newly appointed as our fifth prime minister in four years. I didn’t watch this historic scene live on BBC News. Instead, I saw a 10-second clip on TikTok, with a viral Love Island soundbite: “A hot new bombshell has entered the villa.” Not exactly the introduction you might expect from a world leader – or is it?

The video sent millions of eyes rolling backwards and many flocking to the comments, cringing at the idea of British politics succumbing to ridiculous social media trends. Critics have called his social media strategy “trivial” and a “distraction”. A
title: A TikTok PM may seem laughable – but reaching young people like me might just keep Labour in office | Lucy O’Brien

author: Phil Hoad
description:
Based on a short story by the Goosebumps author, this derivative but tautly plotted tale over-relies on Scooby-Doo-style sleuthery, and its truly unsettling turn comes too late

Adapted from a 1999 short story by Goosebumps’ RL Stine, this kid-proofed piece of midwestern folk horror borrows merrily from The Wicker Man, Stephen King and Tim Burton. Rattling those influences around in its horn of plenty, it rigs up a taut enough plotline about a New York family arriving in the suspiciously fecund farming outpost of Redhaven. But, even given the horror-lite nature of the enterprise, it doesn’t stake out sufficient fresh territory of its own – until it’s too late.

Snotty skate rat Sam (Bean Reid) moves to Redhaven with his mum, Cassie, (Kendra Anderson) and older brother Finn (Seth Isaac Johnson) where, hitting the local harvest festival, they learn that ornery Farmer Palmer (Kevin McNulty) is the one responsible for miraculously wringing out fresh bounty from the town’s onc
title: RL Stine’s Pumpkinhead review – horror from Goosebumps writer has kid confined inside large fruit

author: Jasper Jolly
description:
Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group is frontrunner to buy Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain

  • Can Harvey Nichols find its way back to being Ab Fab again?

  • Business live – latest updates

Harvey Nichols has warned that it will not be able to survive another year without new investment, as bidders for the Knightsbridge-headquartered department store chain circle.

The retailer’s Hong Kong-based owner, Dickson Poon, put it up for sale in June, with Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group aiming to buy it for about £40m.

Co
title: Harvey Nichols warns it could collapse without rescue deal, as bidders circle

author: Agence France-Presse in Los Angeles
description:
Prosecutors to argue that Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis ordered killing and provided gun in Las Vegas drive-by shooting of rapper

The trial is to begin of a former gang leader over the decades-old killing of the rapper Tupac Shakur, one of the most high-profile unresolved murders in the US.

The proceedings, which begin in Las Vegas on Monday and are expected to last a month, are unlikely to make clear who fired the shots that killed the hip-hop legend on 7 September 1996 while he was in the city to see a Mike Tyson boxing match.

Continue reading...
title: Trial of former gang leader to begin over Tupac Shakur murder

author: Julia Kollewe
description:
Temporary vacancies rise for first time in two years, permanent job placements stabilise and temporary billings rise further

Rob Wood, chief economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said rising employment and wage gains suggest the Bank of Engand’s monetary policy committee needs to be cautious.

There may be an element of a “Burnham Bounce” in the survey, as the drop in temporary hiring and rise in permanent in July—usually a sign of falling uncertainty—sits oddly with the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East in July. So Sentiment could easily drop back somewhat.

Wage growth accelerated to the strongest since January, and the permanent salaries index lies above the 52.3 average seen in 2025, suggesting there has been no slowdown in pay growth over the past 18 months. Vacancy growth recovering and staff availability high but easing slightly also point to a labour market beginning to steady.

Despite ongoi
title: UK employment market shows ‘rays of light’ for jobseekers with upturn in pay, study shows - business live

author: PA Media
description:
Met Office considers amber or red warning as forecasters say Thursday is likely to be hottest day of the week

Temperatures could reach 36C (97F) or higher this week, forecaster have said, with possible disruption to railway lines and power networks as the Met Office considers issuing rare amber or red extreme heat warnings.

Parts of the UK are forecast to experience their fifth heatwave of the summer as the country continues to bake in an unprecedented period of dry, hot weather.

Continue reading...
title: UK temperatures could hit 36C as fifth heatwave of summer looms

author: Aaron Bower
description:
Record 10-time Super League champions are poised to miss out on playoffs for the first time but their problems run deeper than poor results

Perhaps the biggest concern as the full-time hooter sounded on another miserable evening for St Helens on Thursday was that the anger, along with thousands of supporters, had long since disappeared and had been replaced with a sense of apathy.

No club have been as consistent a force in the history of Super League quite like Saints. Wigan were almost relegated 20 years ago, Leeds have finished in the bottom half on multiple occasions and the other two champions, Bradford and Hull KR, have spent extended spells outside of Super League. And that is why this is such a story.

Continue reading...
title: St Helens’ decline reaches breaking point with stench of failure lingering

author: Rachael Healy
description:
She started standup at 17 playing ‘unsafe basements’ and braving revolting hecklers – and even worse headline acts. Now she writes for SNL and is giving Edinburgh a blast of her surreal comedy

Comedy isn’t just a career for Bella Hull. It’s a compulsion. “Standup for me is like – I have to do it,” says Hull, who first picked up a mic aged 17. “Regardless of what the response is.”

A decade in, the response is resoundingly positive. The 28-year-old had a sell-out show at last year’s Edinburgh fringe (Doctors Hate Her, which explored a break-up, insanity and the occult), appearances on Have I Got News For You and The News Quiz, and a coveted role as writer on the new UK version of Saturday Night Live. “There’s something symbolic about being the person with the voice,” she says of standup. “A lot of situations in my personal life, I don’t
title: ‘Men have 30 seconds to get a laugh. Women have 10’: standup Bella Hull on proving herself in rough clubs

author: Arifa Akbar
description:
Pleasance Dome, Edinburgh
Jacob Sparrow’s award-winning two-hander finds hope and humanity amid the prejudice and loss of the 1990s

One of the highlights of the Edinburgh international festival is a revival of Tony Kushner’s Angels in America, an era-defining play set at the height of the Aids crisis. In a smaller room of the same city is Jacob Sparrow’s debut – an award-winning two-hander that captures the desperation and hope of young men with Aids in the 1990s.

It is a miniature piece, relatively speaking, and surprisingly uplifting, given the subject matter. The setup is apparently inspired by the real-life public furore around plans to build an Aids hospice in a Suffolk village. Sparrow’s characters, both gay and at close quarters with HIV, ruefully mention the fears in this village around the potential contamination of their cows if the hospice were to be built.
title: Sanctuary review – tender, uplifting portrait of love in the Aids crisis

author: Anna Tims
description:
A leak beneath our fridge-freezer last winter caused extensive damage but there’s still no functioning kitchen

Eight months after reporting a leak to our home insurer, Hastings Direct, my husband and I and our two-year-old are still effectively homeless.

Last winter, we discovered that an unnoticed leak beneath our fitted fridge-freezer had caused extensive damage to the floorboards of our kitchen/living room.

Continue reading...
title: Hastings Direct’s failures forced my family out of our home

author: Xan Brooks
description:
This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of Seeing

The cultural critic John Berger was still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. From his home in the Alps, he proceeded to liaise with the collection’s curator, Tom Overton, sorting each item and recounting the wild stories behind them. When Overton sought permission to write Berger’s biography, though, the critic insisted that he wait a few years. Death changes the relationship between the writer and his subject. More often than not, it complicates and enriches it. Berger – who spent much of his career in passionate conversation with the past – probably knew that better than anyone.

Berger typically described himself as a storyteller, an elastic job title which allowed him to swing between fiction and poetry, essays and screenplays. Implicitly, too, the term helped frame his cri
title: John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering critic

author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
description:
Novel squat Android opens to an iPad-like screen for video or multitasking, with plenty of power and battery life

Samsung’s latest folding phone breaks the mould with a squat, passport-like shape reminiscent of the Blackberry, which opens up to become a tablet similar to an iPad mini. It is certainly a better shape for a tablet than other designs, but is a short and wide phone when closed a compromise too far?

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is an entirely new variant in Samsung’s foldable family for this year launched alongside the Z Fold 8 Ultra with a more familiar candy bar shape. Both folders are extremely expensive, with the Fold 8 starting at £1,699 (€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699) and the Fold 8 Ultra at £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), with RAMageddon driving up prices even at the top of the market.
title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: your passport to a folding phone future

author: Hannah J Davies
description:
Matt Baker invites celebrities to talk about their pets. Plus, US soccer legend Megan Rapinoe makes her hosting debut

This series by Blue Peter and One Show alumnus Matt Baker is a wholesome entry into the well-worn celebrity interview genre. Indeed, it’s hard to be too cynical when you’re listening to Bill Bailey detail his menagerie, which has included everything from parrots and lizards to armadillos and the dog he is ostensibly on the show to talk about, a Japanese chin named Chocho. Other guests for this run include Martin Clunes and Clare Balding.
Widely available, episodes weekly

Continue reading...
title: Wholesome animal chat that will melt your cynicism: best podcasts of the week

author: Sarah Rodrigues
description:
The spa town of Balatonfüred is a bucolic gem for sailors, hikers … and wine lovers. A new hop-on, hop-off bus tour offers a chance to get a taste of its little-known wineries

The 90-minute train journey south-west from Budapest to the spa town of Balatonfüred unveils a landscape that segues from gritty industrial compounds to long sweeps of golden sunflowers and fields of pale grain. The carriage is pleasingly retro, with thick velour upholstery; windows that open, awkwardly, with a stiff metal lever; and a bushy eyebrowed conductor replete with ticket machine slung over his shoulder.

But the real retromania is yet to come. Arriving at Balatonfüred station, I board a 1984 DAF bus, painted an almost audacious shade of green. From the open-air rear, I take in the view over Lake Balaton, central Europe’s largest freshwater lake, often referred to as the “Hungarian Sea”.

Con
title: A slow, boozy bus tour of Hungary’s secret vineyards

author: Sarah Gilbert
description:
Spanning generations and multiple Indigenous societies and nations, In Light and Shadow traces the visual importance of Indigenous photographers. Representing work in different genres, the book presents more than 250 images with an accompanying exhibition at Obscura Gallery from 14 August

Continue reading...
title: An indigenous photographic history of America – in pictures

author: Cath Clarke
description:
When discontented Lily becomes a fantastical sea creature her low-budget transformation is strikingly unconvincing, rather in tune with the whole film

Mermaidcore comes to the Welsh coastline in this somewhat stilted family movie about a teenager called Lily who turns into a mermaid. You could imagine it being developed into a series for kids’ TV but as a film it unfortunately falls at the first hurdle – failing to pull off a convincing mermaid transformation. Poor Lily’s shimmering tail is very obviously made from nylon that becomes very clingy when wet, making her legs very visible under the scales.

Ellie Bindman plays Lily, who has moved from London to the Welsh seaside with her family for her stepdad’s work. Resentful about leaving her friends, she is huffy, communicating with her mum Claire (Marie Wilson) primarily in eyerolls. Lily’s only friend in town is Shane (Jack Taruschio Thomas), an awkward, slightly odd trainee local reporter who is following a lead about
title: Mermaid Beach review – Wales gets its mermaidcore moment in teen-empowerment tale

author: Paula Cocozza
description:
Darren Miles had skateboarded all his life. But in his 50s, he realised he was losing his skills and flexibility. So he took it in a new direction

Darren Miles never thought he would compete in any sport for Britain. But in October, he will represent Great Britain in slalom skateboarding – a form of downhill racing – at the World Skate Games in Paraguay. Last week, he completed his World Anti-Doping Agency awareness training. He had to tick a box confirming: “I’m an international athlete.”

“Justification” is the word that comes to mind, he says. “A feeling that I haven’t wasted my life skateboarding, that diverging into something new” – he took up slalom in his late 50s – “and working hard at it has yielded a result of which I am very proud.”

Continue reading...
title: A new start after 60: I took up slalom skateboarding – and I’m off to the world championships!

author: Hollie Richardson, Phil Harrison, Priya Elan, Hannah Verdier and Hannah J Davies
description:
This zany time-travelling show is a bit like Doctor Who: The Sitcom. Plus, Martin and Roman Kemp take an Irish road trip. Here’s what to watch this evening

10.10pm, Sky Comedy
A zany sci-fi comedy that is a bit like Doctor Who: The Sitcom. Warren has a mysterious glittering portal in his shed, but he only ever uses it to dump leaves in. When his teenage daughter is sucked into it one day – leaving her trusty vape behind – he jumps in after her. They find themselves in 2043, where evil refrigerators are trying to kill them (yes, refrigerators). From there, they end up in lots of trouble across different dimensions. Hollie Richardson

title: TV tonight: killer fridges on the loose in a new sci-fi comedy

author: Richard Adams Education editor
description:
Exclusive: Analysis finds cost of higher education ‘falls overwhelmingly on the individual’

The government is piling mountains of debt and higher tax rates on young people heading to university, according to analysis into the “ticking timebomb” of costs faced by future students.

Hundreds of thousands of sixth formers will receive their A-level results on Thursday, with many expecting to continue on to higher education courses.

Continue reading...
title: Students face ‘ticking timebomb’ of debt and higher taxes

author: Steven Morris
description:
Concerns about feeling pressure to have caesarean section, or paying for hotel in Exeter after hospital in Barnstaple suspends birthing services

For mother-to-be Harriet Knight, the suspension of maternity services at one of England’s most remote hospitals means having to face horribly stark choices.

“The next closest maternity unit is a full two hours away and we have a family history of labour taking under two hours from start to finish,” said Knight.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in Devon

author: Brian Logan
description:
Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh
The fast-talking comic considers fraternity culture, gender discrimination and an unrequited crush in a cleverly engineered show

From the outset, Olga Koch’s show Fat Tom Cruise looks like it’s got something meaningful to say. It’s not just the screens and sleek stage furniture, on to which details of several US legal cases are projected (alongside many a glib punchline, admittedly). It’s also our host’s swaggering authority: Koch powers through her show like a woman on a mission. So what’s its agenda, this new set that professes to tell a story that really isn’t Koch’s own? Well, to begin with, it’s that men’s self-esteem issues are laughable and that “teenage girls are more emotionally intelligent than any man”.

Hmm, I thought. Until, in due course, Koch is
title: Olga Koch: Fat Tom Cruise review – surefire standup pirouettes through the punchlines

author: Agence France-Presse
description:
Observatory says 36.9C posted on Sunday is city’s highest official temperature since its records began 142 years ago, with storm driving intense heat in region

Hong Kong has officially recorded its highest ever temperature as Typhoon Dolphin swept warm air over the city, the meteorological service said.

The city’s weather observatory posted a temperature of 36.9C on Sunday, the highest recorded since records began in 1884, the Hong Kong Observatory said in the afternoon.

Continue reading...
title: Hong Kong records hottest day ever as Typhoon Dolphin fuels heatwave
